tracks.title: I Am a Fugitive from a Georgia Chain Gang

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: For the price of a ticket, any moviegoer could witness sophistication and glamour in films like Grand Hotel (1932) and Trouble in Paradise (1932), or learn about the lives of great men such as Louis Pasteur and Emile Zola through biopics. With Citizen Kane (1941), audiences could step into the world of a contemporary celebrity, press baron William Randolph Hearst.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Every so often, the major studios felt ready to educate audiences about some of the darker aspects of American society. In 1931, Warner Bros. bought an autobiographical article by Robert Elliott Burns that had run in True Detective magazine and was later published as the book I Am a Fugitive from a Georgia Chain Gang.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Citizen Kane, the directorial debut of Orson Welles (1915-1985), has always been considered "the greatest film of all time", which makes it hard to assess clearly. Myths have formed around it: that Welles pioneered a series of innovative filmmaking techniques, and that the film was dismissed on its release for being considered too pretentious.
segments.text: Citizen Kane, the directorial debut of Orson Welles (nineteen fifteen to nineteen eighty-five), has always been considered "the greatest film of all time", which makes it hard to assess clearly. Myths have formed around it: that Welles pioneered a series of innovative filmmaking techniques, and that the film was dismissed on its release for being considered too pretentious.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Welles was not the first to use techniques such as greater depth of field, sets with visible ceilings, overlapping sound, jump cuts, "naturalistic" dialogue in which lines trample over one another, chiaroscuro lighting, or a narrative with multiple points of view - although no other filmmaker had dared to combine them with as much fervor and aesthetic creativity as he did.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: When Citizen Kane opened, most critics received it enthusiastically, but its release was sabotaged. Press baron William Randolph Hearst had no trouble at all recognizing himself in the character of Charles Foster Kane. In the blink of an eye, his entire powerful public relations machine went into action against Welles's film, making sure it never got a decent release.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: For such a revolutionary work, the message behind the film is surprisingly conventional: the rich are not to be envied for their wealth, because they have lost the simple pleasures of true love and happiness. Even so, it deserves its top status, first, because Welles's signature is so captivating, stamped so indelibly on every frame, and second, because today viewers can recognize much of Welles in the protagonist himself.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Citizen Kane is still a hugely important film, but amid its visual grandiloquence, its baroque showmanship and its ostentatious techniques - however fascinating they may be - we can hear, like a terrible premonition, the howl of frustration and creative blockage that the future held in store for the brilliant Welles.

tracks.title: I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Despite doubts about the subject matter—one director dismissed it on the grounds that it was unsuitable at a time when people in general were so depressed that many were "jumping out of windows"—the studio persisted, and Burns, though technically still a fugitive from justice, was secretly hired to work on a first draft of the screenplay. The success of I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang (1932), directed by Mervyn LeRoy (1900-1987) and starring Paul Muni (1895-1967) as the fugitive James Allen, incisively exposed the cruelty of the penal system in the American South.

segments.original: Fritz Lang (1890-1976) delivered a powerful indictment of another sordid American secret. Fury (1936) was inspired by the true story of a double lynching in San Jose three years earlier. Spencer Tracy (1900-1967) plays Joe Wilson, a man wrongly accused of kidnapping a child. When a crazed mob sets fire to the jail, he manages to escape, but pretends to be dead so that those responsible will be charged with murder.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In fact, nearly all the people who were lynched at the time were Black, a fact no studio was interested in publicizing. The singular power of Fury lies in the way viewers find themselves uncomfortably drawn to sympathize with the lynchers, who in turn become victims of an injustice.

segments.original: Frank Capra (1897-1991) offered a more optimistic view of the anxieties of the common man. Historian Robert Sklar attributes the secret of Capra's success to "his ability to convince viewers that they were seeing their own strengths and weaknesses, their own dreams and values—in short, seeing themselves represented on the screen."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Capra's heroes may be victims of corrupt politicians and of capitalism, but they are not outsiders. Portraying the lives of the dispossessed on screen was more problematic. When Darryl Zanuck (1902-1979) acquired the rights to John Steinbeck's (1902-1968) novel The Grapes of Wrath (1939), the plight of the refugees of the Dust Bowl—a series of violent dust storms that devastated the southern United States in the 1930s—was a reality that many were unwilling to face.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: John Ford's (1894-1973) sensitive screen version touched the collective conscience of 1940s moviegoers. Singer Woody Guthrie, who retold the story in song, summed up its importance: "Go see The Grapes of Wrath, pardner... you are the star of that picture. Go and see yourself and hear your own words and your own song."
